messages.subject: Job opening - Quantitative Ecologist, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance
messages.subject_clean: Job opening - Quantitative Ecologist, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have the following job opening on my team:

The Population Sustainability team at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance is seeking a highly accomplished Quantitative Ecologist or Ecological Statistician who brings at least five years of post-doctoral or equivalent professional experience and a strong commitment to applied conservation science. This is a full-time Scientist position that will support our local and global conservation programs. The ideal candidate has a strong background in occupancy and capture–recapture modeling, a solid foundation in general statistical methods, and demonstrated proficiency implementing Bayesian analyses using JAGS, NIMBLE, and/or Stan. Experience with the analysis of movement data (e.g. Hidden Markov Models, Resource Selection Functions) along with spatial or GIS based modeling are highly desirable. They will be comfortable implementing and interpreting statistical models, working with large, complex ecological datasets, and collaborating closely with field biologists and conservation practitioners on study design, data analysis, and publications. This role requires someone who can translate rigorous quantitative analyses into clear, actionable insights that inform wildlife management and conservation decision making and who and can communicate effectively with both scientific and non-technical audiences in a mission driven, interdisciplinary environment.

This is a full-time, permanent position. Applications are open now at this link:

https://jobs.dayforcehcm.com/en-US/sdzwa/CANDIDATEPORTAL/jobs/24941

Thanks,

Mathias

messages.subject: GLLVMs: Advanced multivariate analysis of ecological communities in R
messages.subject_clean: GLLVMs: Advanced multivariate analysis of ecological communities in R
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

We are excited to announce a new advanced course: GLLVMs: Advanced multivariate analysis of ecological communities in R

Dates: 7–10 July

Course website: https://www.physalia-courses.org/courses-workshops/gllvm/

This course introduces Generalized Linear Latent Variable Models (GLLVMs) as a modern, model-based framework for analysing multivariate ecological community data. It provides a statistically coherent alternative to classical ordination methods and integrates ideas from generalized linear models, joint species distribution models, and model-based ordination.

Through lectures and hands-on R sessions, participants will learn how to fit, diagnose, and interpret GLLVMs using the gllvm package, and how to translate results into ecological insight.

Key topics include:

Multispecies GLMs and GLMMs

Joint Species Distribution Models and species co-occurrence

Model-based ordination and comparison with classical methods

Covariates, random effects, and model diagnostics

Interpretation and visualization of multivariate outputs

Best regards,

Carlo

--------------------

Carlo Pecoraro, Ph.D

Physalia-courses DIRECTOR

Is it generally acceptable and just uncommon?

messages.subject: Re: omitting an intercept
messages.body_plain:
Dropping an intercept to achieve convergence is generally a red flag. For proportions or otherwise categorical data, you have to either set a reference category or use sum-to-zero constraints. For example, let's say you have a categorical predictor with three levels. There are three (maybe more) options:
Set one level as reference (intercept) and estimate the "offsets" from this reference for the remaining two categories.
Drop the intercept and estimate the effect of each level. Note that essentially, you're just fitting three intercepts here, one for each level.
Keep the intercept but impose a sum-to-zero constraint on the level effects. This is nice, especially when your model has an arbitrary number of categorical predictors with arbitrary levels. The intercept is interpreted as the average across your levels, and the sum-to-zero constraint on the categorical effects ensures the model is fully identified.
What is your model exactly? I'm guessing you have a redundancy that makes your model not identified.

messages.subject: Re: omitting an intercept
messages.body_plain:
Thanks all!

Its a project I'm providing feedback on, in this case it's dropping an intercept on the detection function in distance sampling because they had random effects that weren't working with the intercept included. In another instance, they had a zero-inflated abundance model and dropped the intercept on the linear model for abundance. The covariates have always been continuous.

My impression was that when the folks I work with were doing this, it was because they over-parameterized a model and/or had too sparse of data for the model they wanted to fit. I just was looking to make sure it's not a practice I'm just ignorant of.

messages.subject: Bayesian Species Distribution Models in R
messages.subject_clean: Bayesian Species Distribution Models in R
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

There is still time to join our upcoming online course and take your species distribution modelling (SDM) skills to the next level with us: https://www.physalia-courses.org/courses-workshops/barts/

Dates: 1-3 July

In this hands-on course, participants will learn how to apply Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) to species distribution modelling and explore powerful R workflows using the embarcadero and dbarts packages.

The course will cover practical approaches for building, interpreting, and applying BART-based SDMs, providing participants with new tools for ecological modelling and prediction.

Join us online and discover how Bayesian machine learning can enhance your SDM workflows!

Best regards,
Carlo

--------------------

Carlo Pecoraro, Ph.D

Physalia-courses DIRECTOR
